title: Helping Kids Manage Big Feelings
hook: Young children can't yet calm themselves down on their own — they borrow your calm. Naming feelings and co-regulating now builds the self-regulation that grows with age.
key_points: Self-regulation is still developing; young kids rely on a calm adult to help them settle — this is called co-regulation.
Emotion coaching helps: notice the feeling, name it, and acknowledge it ('It seems like you're angry we have to leave').
Staying calm yourself is the tool; your steadiness is what a dysregulated child borrows to settle.
Teach simple calm-down strategies — slow deep breaths, a quiet spot, a hug — and the skill strengthens over time.
content_html: When a young child melts down, it's not because they're choosing not to calm themselves — it's because they often can't yet. The brain systems behind self-regulation are still developing, so children rely on a steady adult to help them settle. Researchers and the AAP call this co-regulation: in the moment, your child essentially borrows your calm.
extra_html: A practical AAP-described approach is emotion coaching: notice what your child is feeling, put a name to it, and acknowledge it — something like, "I see you're upset; it seems like you're angry because we have to leave the playground." Naming the feeling helps a child feel understood and makes the emotion more manageable. Pair that with staying calm yourself and teaching simple calm-down tools — slow breaths, a quiet spot, a hug — and self-regulation grows stronger with age and practice. This is general guidance; if big feelings seem unusually intense or persistent, talk to your pediatrician.

related.title: Why Toddlers Have Tantrums
related.hook: Tantrums are a normal part of toddler development — big feelings hitting a brain that can't yet manage them or fully put them into words.

related.title: Positive Discipline: Teaching, Not Punishing
related.hook: Discipline means teaching, not hurting. The AAP's most effective tools are calm consistency, catching good behavior, and clear consequences — and it advises against spanking and harsh words.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'co-regulation' mean for a young child's emotions?

choices.text: A calm adult helps the child settle while their own self-control develops
The child is expected to calm down entirely on their own
Two children calming each other down without any adult

flashcards.explanation_html: Young children's self-regulation is still developing. They borrow a caregiver's calm to settle — and that support builds the skill over time.

flashcards.prompt: What are the basic steps of 'emotion coaching'?
flashcards.back_html: Notice the feeling, name it, and acknowledge it — for example, "It seems like you're angry because we have to leave the playground."
